analysis.one_liner: Redirects Social Security payroll taxes into private mutual fund accounts instead of guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees in November 2007, never received a committee vote or floor action, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced part of Social Security with mandatory personal accounts: every employer would have to take each younger worker's employee share of payroll taxes and invest it in a private mutual fund instead of sending it to the government. At retirement, workers could draw only 10% of the account per year unless they bought an annuity from an insurance company, and guaranteed benefits would shrink sharply for everyone born between 1944 and 1967. It also would have created a new tax on Medicare retirees who did not obtain private health insurance coverage, and would have required regulators to keep at least 150 private mutual funds approved to hold these accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Mutual fund companies would gain a mandatory stream of payroll-tax dollars to manage — the bill requires regulators to keep at least 150 approved funds, with minimum size and track-record requirements that favor large incumbent firms. Insurance companies would gain required annuity purchases at retirement and a new tax pushing Medicare retirees into private coverage. Some employers would gain from payroll-tax relief provisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large mutual fund and insurance companies

how_it_helps.text: Each employer must establish a personal Social Security account for every participating employee and invest the employee's payroll-tax share in a qualified mutual fund the worker designates, with a default fund for workers who do not choose.
Account balances are the property of the worker, cannot be garnished, and pass to designated beneficiaries or the estate on death, so money not spent in retirement can be inherited.
Self-employed individuals can participate by paying half of their self-employment tax into their own account.

If the Social Security escrow fund is projected to hold excess money with no borrowing needed for 10 years, the employer payroll-tax rate would be reduced, and payroll tax would no longer be collected from people past retirement age.
Distributions from personal accounts and payments from qualified annuities would be excluded from federal income tax.
Social Security surpluses would be dedicated by law to reducing the public debt rather than spent on other programs.

analysis.who_pays: Workers under retirement age would bear market risk on money that now buys a guaranteed benefit, and guaranteed benefits would be cut steeply by birth year — down to 6% of the current benefit for those born in 1967. Retirees drawing more than 10% of their account a year would have to buy annuities from insurance companies, and Medicare retirees without qualified health coverage would pay a new tax. Investment fees would come out of workers' accounts.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed old-age benefits are phased down for every birth year from 1944 (98% of the current benefit) to 1967 (6%), a deep cut in the assured portion of retirement income for workers in their 40s and younger at introduction.
Retirees can withdraw at most 10% of their account per year unless they purchase a Board-approved annuity from an insurance company, limiting access to their own money.
The bill imposes a new tax on Medicare retirees who fail to obtain qualified health insurance coverage, adding a penalty on top of Medicare itself.

Account funds can be invested only in Board-designated private mutual funds, and the Board must keep at least 150 funds designated — including at least 75 invested solely in stocks — with a 10-year registration record and $100 million market capitalization floor that favor large incumbent fund companies; fees and expenses come out of workers' accounts.

The Social Security escrow fund would be invested in corporate bonds and debentures rather than Treasury securities, and the bill authorizes borrowing if the fund falls short of its benefit obligations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine appeal is ownership: accounts belong to the worker, can be inherited, and escape income tax, and proponents argue market returns would beat the current benefit formula. But the cost side is heavy and lands on the same workers the ownership argument is pitched to: assured benefits are cut by up to 94% depending on birth year, retirement income becomes exposed to a market downturn right before retirement, access to the money is capped at 10% a year, and the design guarantees a large, permanent fee stream to fund companies and annuity sellers chosen by the Board rather than by workers at large. The mandatory health-coverage tax on Medicare retirees is a separate cost with no offsetting benefit spelled out in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five House committees and then to three subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake (R-AZ) introduced the bill on November 14, 2007.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Budget, Energy and Commerce, and Rules Committees on the day of introduction.

Within the following week it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittees on Health and on Income Security and Family Support, and later to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
No markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing Social Security benefit formula and Medicare rules stayed unchanged, and the mutual fund and insurance industries did not receive the new mandatory channel for payroll-tax dollars the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers with guaranteed benefits; fund firms got nothing

for.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SMART Act of 2007 on November 14, 2007.

for.name: 6 House Republicans and 1 House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 6 Republicans and 1 Democrat signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (chaired by a Democrat in the 110th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Income Security subcommittees and never scheduled a markup or vote; no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was Republican and 6 of the 7 cosponsors were Republicans; with Democrats holding the House majority and the committee gavels, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: Every worker's payroll-tax contribution would have been routed into a Board-designated private mutual fund, with a legal requirement to keep at least 150 approved funds — a permanent, mandatory revenue stream. Qualification rules (10-year track record, $100 million minimum size, caps per investment manager) favor large incumbent firms, and management fees come out of workers' accounts.

Retirees drawing more than 10% of their account a year would have to buy Board-approved annuities from insurance companies, and Medicare retirees would face a new tax unless they obtained qualified private health coverage — both create captive demand for insurance products.

Employers would face new duties to set up and administer accounts, with civil penalties up to $50,000 (or $1,000 per employee) for failures, but they would also gain from payroll-tax relief if the escrow fund ran a surplus and from ending payroll tax on workers past retirement age.
